title: Emergent $s+id$ Superconductivity from the Interplay between Electronic Correlations and Electron-Phonon Coupling in $\mathrm{R}_{1-x}\mathrm{Sr}_x\mathrm{NiO}_2$
authors: Zi Yuan, Jun Zhan, Xianxin Wu, Shaozhi Li
abstract: Recent tunneling measurements on infinite-layer nickelates have revealed spatially varying superconducting symmetries, whose microscopic origin remains unclear. Motivated by this observation, we investigate the interplay between electron correlations and electron-phonon interactions in infinite-layer nickelates by combining first-principles calculations with the fluctuation-exchange-Migdal-Eliashberg theory. Our calculations show that spin fluctuations yield robust $d$-wave superconductivity on the Ni $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital, whereas electron-phonon coupling induces $s$-wave pairing on an interstitial orbital, leading to an $s+id$ superconducting state. The emergence of the $s$-wave component is strongly carrier-density dependent: an intermediate electron-phonon coupling of $λ=0.4$ stabilizes the $s+id$ state at $n=0.9$ but not at $n=0.8$. These results imply that local oxygen defects tune the local electron density and form finite-size domains with distinct pairing symmetries, offering a compelling explanation for the spatially inhomogeneous superconducting symmetries observed in experiments.
summary: This theoretical study investigates how the combination of electronic correlations and lattice vibrations dictates superconducting symmetry in nickelates. By applying advanced many-body techniques, the authors predict that spin fluctuations favor d-wave pairing while electron-phonon coupling induces s-wave pairing, resulting in a mixed $s+id$ state. This mechanism offers a quantitative explanation for the experimentally observed spatial inhomogeneity of superconductivity.
main_problem: The study aims to determine the microscopic origin of spatially varying superconducting symmetries observed experimentally in infinite-layer nickelates, moving beyond simple d-wave models.
main_result: The interplay between spin fluctuations (driving d-wave pairing) and electron-phonon coupling (inducing s-wave pairing) leads to a mixed $s+id$ superconducting state. This $s$-wave component is highly sensitive to carrier density, suggesting local defects can explain observed symmetry variations.
method: The authors combine first-principles calculations with the Fluctuation-Exchange–Migdal-Eliashberg (FLEX–ME) theory to model pairing mechanisms.
model_or_system: The system is infinite-layer nickelates ($\mathrm{R}_{1-x}\mathrm{Sr}_x\mathrm{NiO}_2$), modeled using a two-orbital approach that incorporates on-site Coulomb repulsion ($U_d$) and electron-phonon coupling ($\mathcal{H}_{	ext{eph}}$) involving the oxygen $A_{1g}$ phonon mode.
key_observables: Superconducting order parameters ($\Phi_d$ for d-orbital, $\Phi_s$ for IO orbital), superconducting transition temperatures ($T_{c}$), and SC gaps (measured in meV).
important_parameters: Electron-phonon coupling strength ($\lambda$), carrier density ($n$), and the specific phonon mode involved ($A_{1g}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on combining DFT calculations with FLEX–ME theory, which captures both spin fluctuation (d-wave) and charge fluctuation/e-ph (s-wave) pairing contributions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phonon properties, phase diagrams showing SC regimes vs. $\lambda$ for fixed $n$, and temperature dependence of the superconducting order parameters ($\Phi_d, \Phi_s$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the physical system (nickelates) and the theoretical framework (FLEX–ME theory). It then calculates the contributions from spin fluctuations (d-wave) and e-ph coupling (s-wave), culminating in the prediction of an $s+id$ state whose stability depends critically on carrier density.
why_interesting: The explicit inclusion of electron-phonon coupling alongside strong electronic correlations to predict a mixed pairing symmetry ($s+id$) provides a rich, multi-faceted model for unconventional superconductivity mechanisms relevant to condensed matter theory.
